lessons.title: Fixed Assets Concepts and the Asset Lifecycle

slots.practicalActivity: Using fictional Meridian Fabrication Co., list three purchases it might make in a single month: one that should clearly be capitalized as a fixed asset, one that should clearly be expensed, and one that's genuinely borderline given a $5,000 capitalization threshold -- justify the borderline call in one sentence. Then write the five-stage asset lifecycle (Addition, Capitalization, Depreciation, Adjustments/Transfers, Retirement) from memory and name which Oracle Fusion Assets work area you'd use for each stage.
slots.deliverable: A 3-purchase capitalize/expense/borderline classification for Meridian, plus a 5-stage lifecycle-to-work-area reference you wrote from memory.

slots.practicalActivity: Design an asset-book structure for Meridian Fabrication Co.: name one corporate depreciation book and at least two asset categories it would need (for example Machinery and Office Equipment), and for each category specify a plausible default depreciation method, useful life, and GL account set at the category-book level. Explain in one sentence why getting these category defaults right now saves rework once Create Accounting starts running in Chapter 6.
slots.deliverable: A Meridian asset-book and category-defaults table (method, life, and GL accounts per category) with a written justification.

lessons.title: Asset Locations and Asset Key Flexfields

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian Fabrication Co. operates a headquarters office and two production plants. Define a location hierarchy for all three sites, then design a key flexfield structure (at least 3 segments, such as Plant, Department, and Asset Type) that would let a physical-inventory audit instantly tell where any given asset number is supposed to be sitting.
slots.deliverable: A 3-site location hierarchy plus a 3-segment asset key flexfield structure for Meridian Fabrication Co.

slots.practicalActivity: Using Meridian Fabrication Co.'s $120,000 CNC machine (10-year life, $20,000 salvage value), calculate year-one depreciation under straight-line by hand. Then calculate year-one and year-two depreciation under a flat 20% rate applied against net book value, and write one sentence on which method is more appropriate for Meridian's financial statements and why.
slots.deliverable: Worked straight-line and two-year flat-rate depreciation calculations for Meridian's CNC machine, with a written method recommendation.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian's CNC machine from the previous slot ($10,000/year steady-state straight-line depreciation) is placed in service on August 15, not January 1. Using a prorate convention you choose and justify, calculate how much depreciation it should actually receive in its first partial fiscal year. Then explain, in your own words, why depreciation books need their own fiscal-year calendar separate from the corporate GL calendar.
slots.deliverable: A worked first-year prorated depreciation calculation for the CNC machine, plus a written explanation of why depreciation books keep a separate fiscal calendar.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian needs the Machinery category to default to straight-line depreciation in its corporate book, but an accelerated table-based method in a separate tax book, since the two serve different reporting purposes. Specify both sets of category defaults side by side, and write 2-3 sentences explaining why a company runs the same physical asset through two different books that calculate two different depreciation numbers for the same period.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side corporate-book vs. tax-book category-default specification for the Machinery category, with a written explanation of why both exist.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian buys a $3,200 laptop for a new engineer, paid in cash outside Payables. Walk through, field by field, what you'd enter to add it manually (category, cost, date placed in service, location) versus what the same addition would look like through Quick Additions instead, and write 2-3 sentences on when a consultant would recommend one approach over the other.
slots.deliverable: A field-by-field manual-addition entry plus a Quick-Additions comparison for the same $3,200 laptop purchase, with a recommendation on which approach to use when.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian's Payables team pays a $45,000 invoice for a new injection-molding machine, coded to the 'Machinery Clearing' asset clearing account. Walk through, in writing, everything that has to be true about that invoice before Create Mass Additions picks it up, where the line lands afterward (and why that doesn't mean an asset exists yet), and what you'd review and fill in during Prepare Mass Additions before it's ready to post.
slots.deliverable: A written step-by-step trace of the $45,000 injection-molding machine invoice from Payables eligibility through the Prepare Mass Additions review.

lessons.title: Capitalization and Placing Assets in Service

slots.practicalActivity: Continue the $45,000 injection-molding machine scenario: run Post Mass Additions to turn the prepared line into a real depreciating asset record, then decide its date placed in service given that the machine arrived on March 10 but wasn't installed and operational until April 2. Justify which date you'd use and what it changes about the depreciation that starts running.
slots.deliverable: A posted-asset record summary for the injection-molding machine plus a justified date-placed-in-service decision and its depreciation impact.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Adding Assets: pick a new $60,000 piece of equipment for Meridian Fabrication Co. and write one continuous walkthrough from invoice to depreciating asset -- the Payables coding to an asset clearing account, Create Mass Additions, Prepare Mass Additions (category, location, life), Post Mass Additions, and the capitalization/date-placed-in-service decision -- without skipping a step.
slots.deliverable: One continuous written invoice-to-depreciating-asset walkthrough for a new $60,000 Meridian equipment purchase, covering every lesson in the Adding Assets chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the monthly depreciation process for Meridian's CNC machine in draft mode first (recalling the straight-line calculation from an earlier slot), identify what you'd check before rolling it to final, and then write a scenario where a depreciation adjustment is needed afterward -- for example, a useful-life correction discovered after two years -- and explain how that changes the remaining depreciation schedule.
slots.deliverable: A draft-vs-final depreciation run checklist for the CNC machine, plus a worked depreciation-adjustment scenario and its effect on the remaining schedule.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian discovers a $2,000 freight charge that should have been added to the injection-molding machine's cost but was expensed instead. Record the cost adjustment and recalculate the asset's new depreciable basis. Then write a separate scenario where that same machine was originally miscategorized as 'Office Equipment' instead of 'Machinery,' and explain what reclassifying it actually changes (category defaults, GL accounts) versus what it leaves untouched (the depreciation already taken).
slots.deliverable: A worked cost-adjustment recalculation for the molding machine, plus a written reclassification scenario distinguishing what changes from what doesn't.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian revalues a building from a $400,000 net book value up to a $500,000 fair value, with 20 years of remaining life: calculate the new annual depreciation on the revalued basis and identify how much goes to the revaluation reserve. Then, separately, Meridian's specialized packaging line has a $280,000 carrying amount; after losing its only customer, its recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs to sell, or value in use) is now $190,000 -- calculate the impairment loss and write one paragraph explaining why revaluation and impairment are treated so differently even though both change an asset's book value.
slots.deliverable: A worked post-revaluation annual-depreciation calculation for the building and a worked $90,000 impairment-loss calculation for the packaging line, plus a written comparison of the two.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Depreciation and Adjustments: take one Meridian asset through all four adjustment types in sequence within a single written scenario -- a routine depreciation run, a cost-basis correction, a category reclassification, and then a triggering event that forces a choice between revaluation and impairment -- stating which one applies and why, and recalculating net book value after each step.
slots.deliverable: One continuous written scenario running a single asset through a depreciation run, a cost adjustment, a reclassification, and a revaluation-or-impairment decision, with net book value recalculated at each step.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian physically moves the CNC machine from Plant 1 to Plant 2 -- record that as an asset transfer using the location hierarchy you built earlier in this course. Then, separately, Meridian's 20-unit shelving asset ($500/unit, $10,000 total) has 5 units damaged and scrapped with no proceeds and no removal cost: calculate the cost being retired and explain whether this is a full or partial retirement and why the remaining 15 units keep depreciating afterward.
slots.deliverable: A recorded location-to-location asset transfer for the CNC machine, plus a worked partial-retirement cost calculation for the shelving asset.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian's retirement of the 5 shelving units from the previous slot turns out to be a mistake -- they were actually repairable, not scrapped. Walk through what reinstating them should restore (cost, accumulated depreciation) and what it cannot undo. Then take a separate retirement where Meridian sells a $40,000 asset with $32,000 of accumulated depreciation for $12,000 cash, and calculate the gain or loss on retirement.
slots.deliverable: A written reinstatement scenario for the shelving units plus a worked gain/loss-on-retirement calculation for the $40,000 asset sale.

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian relocates an entire 30-asset production line from Plant 1 to a newly opened Plant 3. Rather than transferring each asset one at a time the way you did earlier in this chapter, design the mass transaction you'd run instead, naming the selection criteria you'd use to pull exactly those 30 assets and nothing else, and what you'd check in a results report afterward to confirm every asset actually moved.
slots.deliverable: A mass-transaction specification (selection criteria plus post-run verification check) for relocating Meridian's 30-asset production line.

lessons.title: Fixed Assets to General Ledger Transfer

slots.practicalActivity: Meridian runs Create Accounting in draft mode after this period's depreciation run and finds the CNC machine's depreciation expense pointing at the wrong department's account -- the kind of category-default mistake made all the way back in Depreciation Setup. Explain why catching this in draft mode matters so much more than catching it after the Fixed Assets to General Ledger transfer, then write the actual debit/credit entries Create Accounting should generate once the account is fixed.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of the draft-vs-final-accounting catch, plus the corrected debit/credit journal entry for the CNC machine's depreciation.

slots.practicalActivity: An external auditor asks Meridian's consultant to prove the Fixed Assets subledger agrees with the General Ledger for the Machinery category this quarter. Name which Fixed Assets report you'd pull to show the asset-by-asset detail, and walk through the reconciliation steps you'd follow to tie that report's total back to the GL account balance, flagging what you'd investigate if the two didn't match.
slots.deliverable: A named audit-ready Fixed Assets report plus a written subledger-to-GL reconciliation walkthrough for the Machinery category.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Meridian's Fixed Assets period-close checklist in order (depreciation run, Create Accounting, GL transfer, reconciliation, close the period) and explain what closing the period actually locks down. Then, using the course's own troubleshooting-practice lesson as your model, pick 3 realistic Fixed Assets problems (a mass addition stuck in the interface table, a reconciliation that doesn't tie, a period that won't close) and write a root-cause-and-fix script for each.
slots.deliverable: An ordered Fixed Assets period-close checklist plus a 3-problem troubleshooting script.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can take an asset through its entire lifecycle in Oracle Fusion Assets -- setting up books, categories, and depreciation defaults; adding assets manually and through mass additions from Payables invoices; running and adjusting depreciation, including revaluation and impairment; transferring and retiring assets with gain/loss calculations; and closing the period by reconciling Assets to the General Ledger.
